Bastille Day

Long before the event, it is said that great legendary warriors overthrew tyrannic lords with the help of our very rightful Marianne, establishing Liberty and Fraternity on every faithful realm. As it is a well-respected and established tradition, it is my duty to invite the fellow lords of my realm to duly celebrate such a divine day.

Austerlitz, London, and Colombey les Deux Église are also holy cities, scarcely inferior to the dignity of Paris and Marseille, and to which the route is safer.

Paris

You reach Paris—the holy city. It was here, many years ago, that Marianne led the furious people of Paris against the perfidious king. It was here that the most important events in the history of the venerable Republic took place—here La Declaration was signed and here that many of Marianne's followers shed blood for the Republic. You pass the ruins of this venerable city—the ruins of the Eiffel Tower, built long before the Event, during the heyday of the Republic—past ancient temples and streets. Soon you reach the Panthéon—the most important place in Paris. You enter and feel the great Frenchmen buried here over the centuries gazing down upon you. You fall to your knees and listen intently to what Marianne expects of you...
Vive la République et Marianna!
Marseille

You reach Marseille – a vast port city unfolds before your eyes. Years ago, it was here that the most loyal legionnaires of the Republic and the Emperor were born, those who died for Marianne. Although Marseille today is not what it was before the Event, it is still a large and impressive city – it was also here that the Jacobins' most sacred anthem, La Marseillaise, was composed. You pass through successive streets and reach the market square – the place where sentences were announced and carried out in Marianne's name. There, you pause for a moment to pay homage to those who stood here and sang this venerable anthem for the first time.
Vive la République et Marianna!
Austerlitz

You reach Austerlitz – an inconspicuous town in Moravia. Today, it's a musty hole near Brno. You see a large field in the distance – there, many years ago, the Emperor defeated the forces of the perfidious Emperor of Austria and proved to him that the forces of Marianne's veneration were capable of resisting the perfidy of kings and tyrants. Then, after strolling through these sacred fields, where so much French blood was shed, you reach the Peace Monument – a large monument crowned with a cross. According to legend, this was the place from which the Emperor commanded his legions. Here, you pay him silent homage, singing "La Chant du Depart".
La victoire en chantant...!
Colombey les Deux Église

You arrive in Colombey les Deux Église, a modest village near Chaumont. To the casual German or English merchant, this town may not seem like much, but for a loyal follower of the General, it is the most important city, after Paris and Marseille. It was here, many years ago, that the General was born—the man who saved the Republic from the perfidious German tyrants. First, passing the town's modest houses, you stand before his monument—a large Cross of Lorraine, the symbol worn by legionnaires years ago. Then you visit his childhood home, known as La Boisserie, where he was born. Despite many years, it has not suffered much damage and is cared for by locals who fervently worship Marianne and the General. Soon, you enter the house to pay your respects, along with the others gathered there.
Général, nous sommes avec vous...
London

You arrive in London—the largest city in England and the ancient capital of this country. You see many old buildings—Westminster Abbey, Buckingham Palace, and others—but you are interested in only one place: the Banqueting House. It was in front of this house, many years ago, before the Emperor and the General began their wars, that the English, enlightened by Marianne, overthrew their tyrant king, Charles I, and guillotined him, according to legend. So you walk up to the house—there you see many people, both locals and visitors from all over the world. You approach to pay silent homage to Cromwell and his companions, who overthrew the perfidious tyranny of the Stuarts.
Vive la Cromwell!

Republican Bureaucracy

The system of republican bureaucracy perpetuated by the Jacobins stems from the legacy of the pre-Event French Republic, which, as a unitary state, was divided into a series of administrative units: regions, departments, arrondissements, cantons, and communes. This system of government is characterized by a strict hierarchy at each administrative level and a lack of strict division between nobility and peasantry.

Gallican

The origins of the Gallican Church date back to the time before the Event, when French priests and bishops developed a belief that national customs were above universal canon law, and that the pope had a ruling voice only in matters of faith and morals, not in disciplinary matters. After the rise of Jacobinism, most Gallicans supported the Revolution. Although Gallicanism declined centuries before the Event, it was revived after the Event when the last bishop of Orleans, in communion with Rome and in agreement with the Jacobins, declared himself pope of a new, licensed church operating in Jacobin-controlled countries. Today, the Gallicans still maintain the supremacy of the council over the pope and express full support for the Jacobins' postulates.

School of Lamennais

This character follows the theological school of Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand, a Gallican saint and Doctor of the Church, whose theology emphasized pragmatism and good relations with non-Christian philosophers, who, according to his theology, held seeds of truth in their teachings. Charles-Maurice was renowned for serving as advisor and chancellor to the Emperor during the early years of the Revolution, a Jacobin hero who fought against the forces of perfidy.

This character follows the theological school of Blaise Pascal, a Gallican saint and Doctor of the Church, whose theology emphasized mysticism and a complete recognition of oneself as powerless against God's will. Among the Gallicans, this school is the furthest removed from orthodox Catholicism, emphasizing poverty of spirit and of the Church, as well as the conviction that we are but dust of the earth, and that all beautiful things, like the Republic, are transient and nothing compared to the "Divine Republic" that will come after the Parousia. Blaise Pascal is known for living in the times before the people, enlightened by Marianne, overthrew tyrannical kings, yet he opposed them with his pen and mouth.

This character follows the theological school of Hugo Lamennais, a Gallican saint and Doctor of the Church. This school is characterized by a particular sympathy for Jacobin ideas. According to its members, it is dogma that all power comes from the people (other schools support this teaching, though they do not accord it the status of dogma), and the papacy was established by the First Lateran Council, it did not exist before, and its power was delegated to it by the Church. Lamennais is known for having been imprisoned for many years by the perfidious and tyrannical King Charles of Bourbon before the venerable Louis-Philippe personally released him, thanking him for his struggle on Marianne's behalf.
Choose Theological School

Since the Gallican Church was established in France as a tolerated Christian church in the Jacobin states, three theological schools have developed which today dominate the theological and pastoral discourse among the Gallicans: the Talleyrand School, which emphasizes dialogue with the neuhumanist philosophies, the Pascal School, which emphasizes mysticism and dialogue with other Christian denominations, and the Lamennais School, which emphasizes the connection between Gallicanism and Jacobinism even more than the other schools.

Walking past a village, you see a large group of peasants in the distance, cheerfully singing the ballad of the cunning Francois, who transformed from a wretch into a detective. This intriguing song stops you for a moment, and those in the distance hear you and call out to you to come over.
Come to them
Ignore them and walk away
Vautrin alias Vidocq

You approach and see the villagers' brightly smiling faces. You sit down next to them, they offer you wine, and they begin to tell you a song about Vautrin, also known as Vidocq, who before the Event was an eternal scoundrel and vagabond. However, enlightened by Marianne, he fell in love with her and fought for her along with other admirers on the fields of glory against the perfidious tyrants who invaded France. He then founded the first detective agency in the world, revolutionizing the art of catching bandits and giving them what they deserve. As the villagers finish their song, you thank them, promise to pray to Marianne for them, and bid them farewell.
Nice story
You approach and see the faces of the villagers more clearly. As you get closer, one of them, the drunkest one, throws a stone at you. The rest, encouraged, soon do the same, and you run away.
Drunken rabble

Walking along the road, you enter the city. As you walk, one of the boys accosts you, inviting you to watch an execution that's about to take place. Without waiting for your opinion, the guy grabs you and leads you to the spot, as if you were the one about to be executed. After a moment, you arrive...
I don't know what I should say...

A young man is being dragged to the gallows. The executioner's pronouncement indicates that he has been convicted of three murders. The crowd cheers widely, expressing both joy at his execution and hatred for him. A local official, who at first glance looks corrupt, watches from afar. The condemned man looks at him, then at the crowd, then at you, and he looks absolutely remorseless.

The condemned man makes the sign of the cross and goes to receive the laurels of martyrdom.

The condemned woman weeps, professes her innocence, and begs for mercy, as if in disbelief that she will day today.

You arrive and see masked bandits attacking people, with trash cans scattered everywhere around the wagon. You join the fray and fight shoulder to shoulder with the hikers against the outlaws. The fight is short but deadly. Out of the corner of your eye, you see the deaths of two hikers and one bandit, and you fight like a madman yourself. A moment later, the bandits flee, and you look at your spontaneous allies, and they look at you: a few richly dressed men and a woman. Suddenly, you feel dizzy, you try to lean against the wagon, but you fall, losing touch with reality...
Oh, beloved Marianne...

After a moment, he tells you that one of these wealthy men, a widower, has something to tell you. You ask the medic to bring him to you. A moment later, the man arrives. He's quite handsome and your age. He tells you that when he saw you in combat, he fell in love with you, seeing you as a brave and beautiful woman. After a moment, he falls to his knees, pulls out a ring, and, to your surprise, proposes to you.

Today, under the influence of many advisors and priests, the rightful President of the Republic, [Root.GetTitledName], has decided that it is high time to reclaim the territory long lost and plundered by the enemies of the homeland. The time of peace and defense has ended, and the time has begun when the French Revolution, begun centuries ago by Marianne and the Emperor, and defended by the General, flourished and, with its roots, destroyed the reactionary, tyrannical, and perfidious neighboring monarchies and false, oligarchic republics.
